result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_assortativity_nominal()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate assortativity for categorical (nominal) node attributes. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L57851-L57976){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_assortativity_nominal(attribute) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Nominal assortativity](/assets/graphs/get-assortativity-nominal.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two triangles joined by one edge, with the nodes split into two categories: A, B, C in the accent color and D, E, F in teal. Six of the seven edges join nodes of the same category, so mixing is assortative and r = 0.714." width="100%"} Measures the tendency of nodes with the same attribute value to connect, also known as homophily. Uses Newman's formula for categorical mixing patterns: it compares the fraction of edges that join nodes of the same category with the fraction you would expect if edges were placed at random given how many edge ends each category has. A single number summarizing "do like nodes link to like nodes?" is useful for: - measuring homophily in social networks (by department, school, party, language) - checking whether communities or clusters line up with a known label - detecting disassortative structure, such as buyer-seller or host-parasite networks, where connections mostly cross categories Attribute values are compared by their string form, so `1` and `"1"` count as the same category. Every edge is counted, including self-loops and parallel edges. For undirected graphs each edge counts in both directions; for directed graphs the mixing matrix is built from source-to-target pairs only. A consequence is that in a directed graph where every edge runs from one category to another (for example, predator to prey) the expected same-category fraction is already zero, so the coefficient is `0` rather than negative. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attribute]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Name of the categorical node attribute to analyze, such as `"group"` or `"country"`. Every node in the graph must have this attribute, and at least two distinct values must occur. Values of any type are accepted (they are compared as strings). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Assortativity coefficient, at most `1`: - `r = 1`: perfect assortativity (only same-type connections) - `r > 0`: assortative (same types prefer to connect) - `r = 0`: random mixing - `r < 0`: disassortative (different types prefer to connect) The minimum value depends on the category proportions; `-1` is reached only in special cases such as a perfectly bipartite undirected graph with two equally sized (by edge ends) categories. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph has no edges, the attribute is missing on any node, there are fewer than two different attribute values, or the edges give no basis for comparison (for example, every edge end belongs to a single category). ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For a categorical attribute this is Newman's *modularity by attribute*: $r = \dfrac{\mathrm{tr}(E) - \|E^2\|_1}{1 - \|E^2\|_1}$, where $E$ is the mixing matrix whose entries $e_{ij}$ record the fraction of edges running between attribute values $i$ and $j$. $r = 1$ means the graph is fully segregated by attribute (only within-class edges); $r = 0$ matches random mixing at the given marginals; negative $r$ signals systematic cross-class connections. This is the tool that formalizes the "birds of a feather" intuition, and negative variants surface bipartite-style structures like predator-prey webs or user-item recommendation graphs. Building the mixing matrix is a single $O(V + E)$ pass. ## Examples {.doc-examples} When most edges connect nodes that share the same categorical attribute (students to students, faculty to faculty), the assortativity coefficient is positive -- a sign of homophily: ::: {#abcc7de6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["Alice", "Bob", "Carol"], group="students") .add_nodes(["Prof1", "Prof2"], group="faculty") .add_edges( [ ("Alice", "Bob"), ("Bob", "Carol"), ("Prof1", "Prof2"), ("Alice", "Prof1"), # One cross-group edge ] ) ) # Returns a positive value: mostly within-group connections g.get_assortativity_nominal("group") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.4666666666666667 ``` ::: ::: Predator-prey relationships show the opposite pattern: predators connect to prey rather than to each other. In an undirected graph where every edge crosses the two categories, the coefficient is strongly negative: ::: {#8053fa75 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["Wolf", "Lion"], type="predator") .add_nodes(["Deer", "Rabbit"], type="prey") .add_edges([("Wolf", "Deer"), ("Wolf", "Rabbit"), ("Lion", "Deer")]) ) # Returns -1.0: every edge joins a predator and a prey g.get_assortativity_nominal("type") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` -1.0 ``` ::: ::: The same edges in a directed graph (all pointing from predator to prey) give `0.0`, because the directed formula expects no same-category edges to begin with. Use an undirected graph when you want to detect this kind of cross-category mixing: ::: {#de0a22e5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g_dir = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["Wolf", "Lion"], type="predator") .add_nodes(["Deer", "Rabbit"], type="prey") .add_edges([("Wolf", "Deer"), ("Wolf", "Rabbit"), ("Lion", "Deer")]) ) # Returns 0.0, not a negative value g_dir.get_assortativity_nominal("type") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.0 ``` ::: :::
